blocks.heading: Scale economies and diseconomies
blocks.text: Scale of operation concerns the size or capacity of business activity. Economies of scale are causes of average-cost reductions as scale increases, such as purchasing advantages, use of specialist equipment or management and spreading suitable fixed costs across more output. Economies of scale lower average cost only when output actually increases and the extra capacity is used. Diseconomies can arise at the same time, so the overall average cost of a growing business may not fall if they cancel out the savings. Diseconomies are causes of average-cost increases beyond a scale, for example communication difficulties, slower decisions or reduced coordination. Total cost can rise while average cost falls, so keep the measures distinct. This concerns business costs, not the economy’s system of ownership and resource allocation.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Hena Packs can negotiate a material discount for larger orders, but rapid expansion also creates stock-control errors. The discount can reduce unit cost if useful sales justify the larger purchase and storage and coordination costs do not offset it. The errors can create diseconomies, so growth is not automatic evidence of lower average cost.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why Hela Packs negotiating a bulk material discount concerns economies of scale rather than a market or mixed economic system.

The discount can reduce unit cost if higher scale and useful sales justify the purchase and coordination or storage diseconomies do not offset savings. Economic systems concern how an economy allocates resources and ownership. The enterprise cost mechanism is a different concept.
